title_original: Madden review – Nicolas Cage is a cartoonish NFL legend in David O Russell’s stinker
excerpt_original: Oscar-nominated director delivers a thoroughly unserious biopic, wasting Christian Bale and Sienna Miller’s talents John Madden was a beloved American original, the burly football coach who segued easily from Super Bowl burnout to television darling to the last name in gaming as…

blocks.text: J ohn Madden was a beloved American original, the burly football coach who segued easily from Super Bowl burnout to television darling to the last name in gaming as the NFL was overtaking baseball as the national pastime. When he wasn’t crashing into family rooms on football Sundays and Thanksgivings to break down the game’s rough complexities into fun-sized morsels, he was pressing flesh with everyday Americans while barnstorming the country in his Madden cruiser – the coach bus he depended on to compensate for his well-documented fear of flying.

That the Madden video game franchise outlived the avuncular Minnesotan , whose death at age 85 in 2021 was mourned throughout the sport, is as much a testament to his singular knack for teaching the game’s fundaments as it is to his willingness to bring his classroom to students, wherever they might huddle. But Madden, a new Amazon biopic that can’t decide whether it’s serious or slapstick, has drawn all the wrong lessons.

The high expectations for Madden extend well beyond its principal subject. Kathryn Hahn, Sienna Miller and Christian Bale headline – with the latter committing hardest to the role of the tracksuit-wearing Oakland Raiders principal Al Davis. And David O Russell’s experience tackling football fandom in Silver Linings Playbook makes him particularly well suited to direct. But instead of a sincere tribute to the coach whose influence and win percentage exceed those of the great Vince Lombardi, Russell’s Madden is closer to the Pop Tarts movie version of the formidable coach’s story than Ben Affleck’s Air , reducing one of the 20th century’s most celebrated pop culture figures to a thin caricature.

What else could Madden be but a disservice to the man after Russell fumbled the lead casting? After Will Ferrell passed, the next man up was the seriously unserious Nicolas Cage, whose method acting effectively stopped at the fat suit and tousled wig. His Madden is a capricious oaf in the Chris Farley mold – rumbling, bumbling and stumbling through every scene as Russell and his co-writers scramble to tick off the major bullets in the coach’s biography: Madden’s abrupt coaching retirement at age 42, the uneasy start to his enduring TV booth partnership with imperturbable play-by-play man Pat Summerall, those first meetings at EA Sports with Trip Hawkins. You’d think John Mulaney would be eager to crow about his prominent role as Hawkins in “a David O Russell film”. And yet when the star standup comedian hosted SNL last week , Madden never came up.

Mulaney knows the film he’s in is a stinker – and so, for that matter, does Miller. She looks like she might crack up at the ridiculousness in early scenes as Raiders first lady Carol Davis. But in her defense: it would be hard for anyone to keep a straight face opposite Bale – who more than justifies the makeup and costuming departments’ considerable efforts to revive Davis, the NFL’s immortal rogue. Bale nails Davis’s Brooklyn accent, the pimp swagger and his roiling insistence on being the smartest guy in the room – right down to diagnosing Madden’s persistent stomach problems as “gas”. Turns out, it was a bleeding ulcer.

It’s Davis’s genuine affection for Madden that makes the character Cage is playing seem remotely human. Even the marriage between Cage’s John and Hahn’s Virginia plays like a Drunk History re-enactment, especially when Russell gets his dreamy set pieces going. But the film saves its most grating frames for Shane Gillis as wacky Madden neighbor Vince McGary, a thoroughly dispensable composite character.

Madden is further at pains to exploit its field access, stitching together re-enactments of classic game highlights with authentic NFL Films – but not seamlessly enough to escape flags from Madden-educated football fans. In one especially glaring scene, Russell has Cage’s Madden in the booth with Summerall in the 1970s, telestrating a classic 1990s NFL highlight of a player’s steaming head. The Fox Sports scorebug and the player, Dallas Cowboys standout Nate Newton, give the game away. The real football tie-ins work slightly better in reverse, with former NFL stars Julian Edelman and Marshawn Lynch playing against type as dweeby EA programmers – that is, until they connect in the company parking lot on a halfback option.

Generally, it’s hard not to see Madden as yet another obvious play by Amazon – this one a desperate bid to reunite the legions who still mourn their favorite football teacher for one more Thanksgiving. But Russell and Cage’s deeply disappointing efforts don’t just ensure that it’s a sad occasion. They kill the guy twice.
Madden is now available on Amazon Prime Video
